frame-lec01-intro.text: Chapter 1: Introduction: what is pattern recognition? | Guided study

steps.label: Chapter 1: Introduction: what is pattern recognition? | Guided study
01 · A computer sees numbers · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: an image can be measured as gray-level numbers; a classifier only handles numbers.

What does a computer actually see?

steps.label: 01 · A computer sees numbers · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: People recognize a dog whatever its pose, color or distance; a computer must first turn the data into numbers. [Added] The analogy has a limit: people judge by experience, computers by numbers.

steps.label: 01 · A computer sees numbers · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Pattern recognition turns data into numbers first, then classifies the numbers.

steps.label: 02 · Five applications, different inputs, one route · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: machine vision, OCR, computer-aided diagnosis, speech recognition, content-based retrieval.

What do these five examples share?

steps.label: 02 · Five applications, different inputs, one route · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: The inputs differ (images, sound, documents, sequences), yet all follow one route: turn the data into numbers, then classify.

steps.label: 02 · Five applications, different inputs, one route · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Different inputs, same route: measure into numbers, then classify.

steps.label: 03 · A feature is one number measured from data · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: five pixel gray levels (100,110,120,130,140) from one region.

Is a feature one number or many?

steps.label: 03 · A feature is one number measured from data · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: A feature is a number measured from the data that describes one property, such as the average brightness of an image.

steps.label: 03 · A feature is one number measured from data · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: A feature is a measured number describing one property of the data.

steps.label: 04 · A feature vector stacks features in a column · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: l features x_1,…,x_l; the superscript T means transpose.

What is each number in the column?

steps.label: 04 · A feature vector stacks features in a column · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: x=[x_1,x_2,…,x_l]^T. Transposing turns a row of numbers into a column.

steps.label: 04 · A feature vector stacks features in a column · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: A feature vector is l features stacked in a column.

steps.label: 05 · A classifier cuts the feature plane into two regions · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: two features (mean gray level, gray-level standard deviation); 32 simulated points.

Which class gets the star? How sure are we?

steps.label: 05 · A classifier cuts the feature plane into two regions · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Each region becomes a 2-D point. The line is computed from the two class means. The star falls on class B’s side but close to the line, so the conclusion is not certain. The data are simulated, not real patients.

steps.label: 05 · A classifier cuts the feature plane into two regions · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: A classifier is a rule that cuts the feature space, one region per class.

steps.label: 06 · The decision is the sign of g · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: g( x)= w^T x+w_0,  w=[1,1.5]^T, w_0=-150.

What does a g close to 0 mean?

steps.label: 06 · The decision is the sign of g · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Decide A if g<0 and B if g>0. The star [120,30]^T has g=15, not far from 0, so its class is not certain. [Added] Memory aid: the decision is just the sign of g.

steps.label: 06 · The decision is the sign of g · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: A classifier’s decision is the sign of g.

steps.label: 07 · Four questions, four design stages · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: four stages: feature generation, feature selection, classifier design, system evaluation.

Which question is easiest to answer by gut feeling?

steps.label: 07 · Four questions, four design stages · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: The example was a shortcut: two useful features found by luck and a line drawn by eye. A real project must answer the four questions more carefully.

steps.label: 07 · Four questions, four design stages · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Designing a classification system means answering four questions in order.

steps.label: 08 · Design is a loop, not a one-way pipeline · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: when evaluation is poor there are two feedback paths: back to selection, or back to generation.

After a poor evaluation, which stage do you revisit first?

steps.label: 08 · Design is a loop, not a one-way pipeline · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Key idea: a loop, not a one-way pipeline. If evaluation is poor, revise an earlier stage. Some methods merge feature selection and classifier design into one problem. [Added] Memory aid: generate, select, design, evaluate; then loop back.

steps.label: 08 · Design is a loop, not a one-way pipeline · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Design is a loop: a poor evaluation sends you back to earlier stages.

steps.label: 09 · Real boundaries are usually not straight lines · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: one set of points, two boundaries: a line and a curve (simulated data).

Which class is surrounded?

steps.label: 09 · Real boundaries are usually not straight lines · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Most real boundaries are curved surfaces rather than lines. [Added] The data here are simulated, only to show the shape.

steps.label: 09 · Real boundaries are usually not straight lines · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: A classifier must draw curved boundaries; a line is not enough.

steps.label: 10 · Evaluation counts the share of wrong decisions · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: the lecture’s linear rule and 32 simulated samples; a misclassification is a sample put in the wrong class.

Is 3 wrong points enough to judge quality?

steps.label: 10 · Evaluation counts the share of wrong decisions · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: System evaluation measures the error rate systematically, not by gut feeling. [Added] The data are simulated; the numbers only show the calculation.

steps.label: 10 · Evaluation counts the share of wrong decisions · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Evaluation counts the share of wrong decisions instead of guessing.

steps.label: 11 · Supervised learning: every sample has a label · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: every training sample has a known class; the medical-image example is supervised learning.

Could we draw this line without the labels?

steps.label: 11 · Supervised learning: every sample has a label · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Every training sample has a known class. We design the classifier from these labelled samples, like exams already graded by a teacher.

steps.label: 11 · Supervised learning: every sample has a label · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Supervised learning: answers given, learn the rule.

steps.label: 12 · Unsupervised learning: no labels, group by similarity · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: feature vectors without labels; examples: satellite land cover, country statistics.

Who names the clusters?

steps.label: 12 · Unsupervised learning: no labels, group by similarity · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Here we only have feature vectors; the task is to find similar points and group them. The groups emerge from the numbers. [Added] Two key choices: how to define “similar”, and which algorithm to use.

steps.label: 12 · Unsupervised learning: no labels, group by similarity · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Unsupervised learning: no answers, find the structure.

steps.label: 13 · Being close does not mean the same class · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: the closest pair of points from different classes in the simulated data.

Which two points are most likely misclassified?

steps.label: 13 · Being close does not mean the same class · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Common misconception: closeness does not guarantee the same class; two nearby points can belong to different concepts.

steps.label: 13 · Being close does not mean the same class · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Nearby does not mean the same class; clustering results need expert judgment.

steps.label: 14 · Semi-supervised: a few labels guide the whole · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: only 4 points keep labels; must-link forces one cluster, cannot-link forbids it.

Why use both labeled and unlabeled points?

steps.label: 14 · Semi-supervised: a few labels guide the whole · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Semi-supervised learning sits between the two: only a few samples are labeled, yet the unlabeled ones still carry structure that helps.

steps.label: 14 · Semi-supervised: a few labels guide the whole · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Semi-supervised learning: a few answers guide the whole.

steps.label: 15 · Three learning settings differ in how many labels · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: the same 32 points; all labeled, none labeled, only four labeled.

When labels are costly, which would you pick?

steps.label: 15 · Three learning settings differ in how many labels · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: By whether training data carry class labels, learning falls into three groups: all, none, or some.

steps.label: 15 · Three learning settings differ in how many labels · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: The three settings differ by labels: all, none, or some.

steps.label: 16 · Book map: supervised first, unsupervised second · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: chapters 2–16; chapter 10 links system evaluation and semi-supervised learning.

Which part do you want to read first?

steps.label: 16 · Book map: supervised first, unsupervised second · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: The book has two parts, supervised first and unsupervised second, linked by chapter 10. It does not cover syntactic pattern recognition; most chapters include MATLAB programs for teaching.

steps.label: 16 · Book map: supervised first, unsupervised second · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Book map: supervised, the chapter-10 link, then unsupervised.

steps.label: 17 · Recap: from numbers and vectors to learning settings · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: features, feature vectors, classifiers, the four-stage loop, three learning settings.

How would you explain pattern recognition in one sentence?

steps.label: 17 · Recap: from numbers and vectors to learning settings · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Pattern recognition assigns an input to a class by its features; design is a loop of generation, selection, design and evaluation; learning is sorted by labels.

steps.label: 17 · Recap: from numbers and vectors to learning settings · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Chapter 1 in one line: measure, classify, loop to improve; the labels decide the setting.

steps.label: 18 · Practice 1: pick your own pattern-recognition example · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: the three parts: input, features, classes.

Which everyday example have you met?

steps.label: 18 · Practice 1: pick your own pattern-recognition example · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: The exercises give problems and hints only; discuss the answers in class or on the board.

steps.label: 18 · Practice 1: pick your own pattern-recognition example · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Think of the input first, then of the numbers you can measure.

steps.label: 19 · Practice 2: separate sunny from rainy photos · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Female: Used on this page: two features x_1,x_2 form the feature vector; the classes are sunny and rainy.

Which feature best separates sunny from rainy?

steps.label: 19 · Practice 2: separate sunny from rainy photos · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: Hint only: think about brightness and color distributions; discuss the answers in class.

steps.label: 19 · Practice 2: separate sunny from rainy photos · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: A good feature separates the two classes.

steps.label: 20 · Practice 3: why semi-supervised helps when labels are costly · 1/3
steps.speakerNotes:
Male: Used on this page: a few labeled samples plus many unlabeled ones.

Where else are labels costly?

steps.label: 20 · Practice 3: why semi-supervised helps when labels are costly · 2/3
steps.speakerNotes: Female: Hint only: when labels are few, what can unlabeled data still tell us? Discuss in class.

steps.label: 20 · Practice 3: why semi-supervised helps when labels are costly · 3/3
steps.speakerNotes: Male: With few labels, unlabeled data still carry structure that helps.
